content: Our six-person home-storage brand sells through a hosted ecommerce storefront. Monthly revenue is $120,000 from 1,500 orders at an $80 average order value. Of those orders, 600 are first orders acquired through $18,000 in paid advertising, so our paid customer acquisition cost is $30; the other 900 are repeat orders. Gross margin after product cost is 60%. Shipping, fulfillment, and payment fees cost another $8 per order. Existing fixed operating costs, including all six salaries, are $36,000 per month. We have $32,000 in cash and no debt. I handle marketing as the founder, but it takes 15 hours a week and I can spare only four. We can hire an in-house marketer at $58,000 a year plus 20% for employer taxes and benefits, with a one-time $2,000 recruiting cost, or retain an agency for $4,500 a month plus $1,500 onboarding. Advertising spend stays at $18,000 under either option. The employee could start in six weeks and own email, ads, and creative; the agency can start next week on a three-month minimum contract but only handles ads, leaving email and creative with me. Neither promises sales growth. Which option, if either, should we choose? Show current monthly operating surplus, each option's recurring and upfront costs, and the extra monthly orders needed to cover the recurring cost at current unit economics with advertising spend held flat. Propose a 90-day decision plan that accounts for cash, ramp time, and the work still on my plate. State assumptions rather than treating repeat purchases or growth as guaranteed.

# Analysis & Recommendation

---

## 1. Current Monthly Operating Surplus

| Line item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Revenue (1,500 × $80) | $120,000 |
| COGS (40%) | –$48,000 |
| **Gross margin** | **$72,000** |
| Shipping / fulfillment / payment (1,500 × $8) | –$12,000 |
| Paid advertising | –$18,000 |
| Fixed operating costs (incl. salaries) | –$36,000 |
| **Operating surplus** | **$6,000 / month** |

---

## 2. Option Comparison

### Option A — In-House Marketer

| Cost element | Amount |
|---|---|
| Salary ($58,000 ÷ 12) | $4,833 / mo |
| Taxes & benefits (20%) | $967 / mo |
| **Recurring cost** | **$5,800 / mo** |
| One-time recruiting fee | $2,000 |
| Time to start | ~6 weeks |
| Scope | Email, ads, creative — full relief |

### Option B — Agency

| Cost element | Amount |
|---|---|
| Monthly retainer | $4,500 / mo |
| **Recurring cost** | **$4,500 / mo** |
| One-time onboarding | $1,500 |
| Time to start | ~1 week |
| Scope | Ads only — email & creative stay with you |
| Minimum commitment | 3 months ($13,500 total) |

### Delta vs. current surplus

| | New monthly surplus |
|---|---|
| Status quo | $6,000 |
| Option A | $200 |
| Option B | $1,500 |

Both options compress your margin dramatically. Neither is "affordable" in the sense of leaving comfortable cushion; the question is which buys you the most operational relief per dollar.

---

## 3. Extra Orders Needed to Cover the Recurring Cost

**Contribution margin per incremental order** (ad spend held flat, so no marginal CAC):

$$\$80 - \$32\text{ (COGS)} - \$8\text{ (ship/fulfill/payment)} = \$40$$

| Option | Recurring cost | Orders needed ($40 each) |
|---|---|---|
| Employee | $5,800 | **145 orders** |
| Agency | $4,500 | **113 orders** |

That's roughly a 10% lift in total order volume (or a 24% lift in first-order volume) just to break even on the new cost. Neither vendor promises that lift.

---

## 4. Recommendation: Hire the Employee

The agency looks cheaper on paper but fails the real test: **it doesn't solve your bottleneck.** You're 11 hours/week over capacity. If ads consume roughly 5–6 of those 15 hours, the agency removes that slice and leaves you still 5–6 hours over on email and creative—work you've already said you can't absorb. You'd be paying $4,500/month to remain partially stuck.

The employee costs $1,300 more per month but removes the entire marketing load, freeing your 11 hours for product, partnerships, or strategy—activities where a founder's time typically returns more than $117/hour (the effective hourly cost of the role).

**Key assumption:** I am treating the 600 paid-acquisition orders and 900 repeat orders as stable, not growing. If repeat rate erodes or ad efficiency drops, the $200 surplus turns negative quickly. That risk exists under either option and under status quo.

---

## 5. 90-Day Decision Plan

### Weeks 1–6 (Pre-Start Phase)

| Action | Why |
|---|---|
| Post the role and begin recruiting now. Budget the $2,000 fee. | Six-week lead time means every day of delay pushes relief further out. |
| Continue running ads yourself at the current $18k spend. | No performance change expected; maintain baseline. |
| Document your weekly marketing workflows (ad ops, email calendar, creative briefs). | Reduces ramp time for the new hire; also reveals what could be cut if you need to tighten spend. |
| Set aside $2,000 from cash for the recruiting fee. Cash drops to ~$30,000; monthly surplus of $6,000 rebuilds it. | Preserves a buffer above ~$30k through the hiring window. |

**Cash check at Week 6:** ~$30,000 + (6 × $6,000 surplus) – $2,000 recruiting ≈ **$64,000**. Comfortable.

### Weeks 7–10 (Ramp)

| Action | Why |
|---|---|
| Employee starts. Run a two-week shadowing/handoff period. | Protects ad performance during transition. |
| You step back from ad management but review spend and CPA daily for the first two weeks. | Catch any efficiency drift early. |
| Employee audits the email program and proposes a 30-day email calendar. | This is the work you've been neglecting; it's also the highest-leverage channel you currently own (zero marginal ad cost, high repeat potential). |
| Define one measurable target for the employee at Day 30: e.g., maintain CPA ≤ $30 and send ≥ 4 email campaigns. | Gives you an objective check-in point. |

**Cash check at Week 10:** ~$64,000 – (1 × $5,800) ≈ **$58,000**. Still healthy.

### Weeks 11–13 (Evaluate / Decide)

| Metric to review | Threshold |
|---|---|
| CPA on paid ads | ≤ $30 (current level) |
| Email send cadence | ≥ 4 campaigns sent |
| Your hours on marketing | ≤ 4 hrs/week |
| Monthly operating surplus | ≥ $0 (even $200 is acceptable at this stage) |

**If all four thresholds are met:** Continue. The role is paying for itself in time relief even without incremental revenue.

**If CPA has risen above $35 or surplus has turned negative for two consecutive months:** Have a corrective conversation. If unresolved by Day 90, consider whether to reduce ad spend to $14–15k (freeing ~$3–4k) or part ways.

---

## 6. Assumptions Stated Explicitly

1. **Repeat orders (900/mo) remain stable.** I have not modeled any uplift from better email marketing, though that is the most plausible path to the 145 extra orders.
2. **Ad efficiency (CPA $30) holds** during the handoff. In practice, a new person managing the account may cause a 10–20% CPA wobble in weeks 1–3.
3. **No revenue growth is assumed.** The 145-order breakeven figure is a hurdle, not a forecast.
4. **Fixed costs stay at $36,000.** The new salary is additive, not a reallocation from that bucket.
5. **The $32,000 cash figure is accurate and unencumbered** (no upcoming tax bills, inventory prepayments, etc.).

---

## 7. Why Not the Agency (or "Neither")?

- **Agency:** Solves ~40% of your time problem at ~78% of the employee's cost. You'd still be doing email and creative in hours you don't have. The 3-month lock-in ($13,500) is nearly half your cash reserve if things go sideways.
- **Neither:** Preserves $6,000/month surplus but leaves you 11 hours/week over capacity indefinitely. That's a slow-burn risk to the business (founder burnout, neglected email list decay, missed creative testing).

The employee is the only option that actually resolves the constraint you described.
